product: Atlas Administration API + MongoDB database connections
defaultRequirement: Build a connector that creates, reads, updates and deletes documents in a client's MongoDB Atlas database.
summary: "Connect to MongoDB Atlas" can mean two different things: managing Atlas itself (clusters, users) through the Admin API, or reading and writing data through a database driver. They use completely different authentication. Neither uses the typical 'Sign in with…' OAuth popup, which matters if your connector platform only supports that.

capabilities.label: Create documents
capabilities.conditions: Needs a database connection string, a database user with write access, and network access from where the connector runs.

evidence.title: Atlas: connect to your cluster (re-check auth options for the client's tier)

capabilities.label: Read documents
capabilities.conditions: Same requirements as create. Needs a long-running server-side process: Atlas's HTTPS Data API has been retired, so a driver connection is required.

capabilities.label: Update documents
capabilities.conditions: Database user needs readWrite on the target database.

capabilities.label: Delete documents
capabilities.conditions: Database user needs readWrite. Deletes are permanent unless the client has backups.

capabilities.label: Manage clusters, users and projects
capabilities.conditions: Authenticate with a service account (OAuth 2.0 client credentials, tokens valid for 1 hour), or with legacy API keys (HTTP digest). Assign only the roles you need. Calls are only accepted from IP addresses on the API access list.

evidence.title: Generate a service account token (1-hour tokens)

clarifications.question: What does the connector need to do in MongoDB Atlas?
clarifications.why: Data access and Atlas management use different APIs, credentials and network rules.

options.label: Read and write data in a database
Manage Atlas itself (clusters, database users, access lists)

effects.conditions: Use an Atlas service account (client credentials). Refresh the token every hour; handle HTTP 401 by requesting a new one.
Two separate credentials: a service account for the Admin API and a database user for data. Keep them separate.

auth.recommended: Database user (username/password via SCRAM) in a connection string for data. Atlas service account (OAuth 2.0 client credentials) for the Admin API.
auth.why: These are the default, widely supported paths. Neither requires a user-facing OAuth consent screen.
alternatives: X.509 certificates, AWS IAM, or OIDC / workload identity federation for database auth. Availability depends on cluster tier and configuration; verify before promising.
Legacy Atlas API keys (digest auth). Prefer service accounts for new work.

blockers.title: Network access list blocks unknown IPs
blockers.detail: Atlas only accepts connections from allowed IPs (or private endpoints). Cloud-hosted connectors and AI agents often have changing IPs.
blockers.resolution: Give the client a fixed egress IP range for the connector, or set up private networking. Avoid 0.0.0.0/0 in production.
blockers.handoff: Hi! To build {requirement}, please add our connector's egress IPs <IP_LIST> to the Atlas project's Network Access list, and create a database user with readWrite on <DATABASE>. Docs: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/security/ip-access-list/

blockers.title: Your connector platform may not support this auth style
blockers.detail: Many connector platforms expect 'authorization code' OAuth with a consent popup. Atlas uses connection strings and client credentials instead.
blockers.resolution: Check your platform supports custom credential fields (connection string, client ID/secret). If not, this is a platform gap, not an Atlas gap.

blockers.title: Needs a server-side runtime
blockers.detail: Drivers keep persistent connections. Serverless or browser-only connectors need connection pooling or a small backend.
blockers.resolution: Run data access in a backend service and reuse the client across requests.

alternatives.option: A small backend using an official MongoDB driver that exposes only the operations you need
alternatives.doesNotCover: Calling MongoDB directly from a browser or no-code tool without a backend

engineering.assumptions: Driver-based CRUD with a database user, fixed egress IP available.

waiting.notes: Depends on the client adding your IPs and creating a database user.

uncertainty: Whether your connector runtime has a fixed outbound IP
Whether the client's security team allows username/password database users
